extracted.intended_audience: scholars and educated readers of anthropology, psychology, and philosophy (19th-century intellectual readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for judging hypotheses about the origin of myths, animal-worship, and moral sentiments — focusing on explanatory power, empirical grounding, developmental evidence, and distinctions between emotional and intellectual processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformitarian explanatory principle
rubrics_metrics.description: True interpretations of natural processes habitually trace them to causes still in action (as in Geology, Biology, Philology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that explanations which refer to ongoing, observable causes are preferable: 'True interpretations of all the natural processes... habitually trace them to causes still in action. It is thus in Geology; it is thus in Biology; it is thus in Philology.' Use present causes as analogues when interpreting past phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory breadth / multiple-phenomena account
rubrics_metrics.description: A true cause should account not only for the particular group of phenomena but also for other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that explain a range of related phenomena (e.g., worship of animals, plants, mountains, winds, celestial bodies, fetichistic conceptions, grammatical gender assignment, compound animals and monsters). The author gives this as a verification: the proposed cause 'equally well explains the worship of animals, of plants, of mountains, of winds, of celestial bodies, and even of appearances too vague to be considered entities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with the general law of evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis should conform to an evolutionary account: showing how one simple, vague, aboriginal form gives rise by continuous differentiations to many heterogeneous forms of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations gain credibility if they fit into a broader evolutionary framework of differentiation and increasing complexity; this is offered as a 'further characteristic of a true cause.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of explanatory gap (continuity with modern thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good hypothesis diminishes the apparent contrast between early modes of thought and our present modes, making primitive ideas intelligible rather than gratuitously absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats increased plausibility (bridging the intellectual gap) as evidence in favor of a hypothesis: 'it immensely diminishes the apparently-great contrast between early modes of thought and our own mode of thought.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical support and problem-solving capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis gains probability when supported by a large mass of evidence and when it yields solutions to many minor problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author promises that 'The large mass of evidence which I shall be able to give... joined with the solutions it will be shown to yield of many minor problems... will give to it a still greater probability.' Favor hypotheses that both accumulate evidence and resolve ancillary anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for apparent anomalies via historical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent contradictions or diverse genealogies (e.g., multiple names for the Sun) should be interpretable as expected consequences of historical processes like nicknaming, migration, and fusion of traditions, rather than dismissed as careless tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat contradictory genealogies as necessarily fatal; treat them as parts of the evidence produced by processes (nicknaming, separate local traditions becoming combined). The author contrasts this approach with Prof. Max Müller's attribution of 'careless' traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly etiquette: accurate representation before criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should accurately represent an author's full exposition and consult relevant prior works before asserting that a doctrine is disposed of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reproaches critics who attack a partial or mis-stated position: 'would it not have been well if he had referred to the Principles of Psychology... before criticising it?' Advises against attacking a straw-man and emphasizes consulting primary sources (e.g., Principles of Psychology) and fuller expositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature polemics; prefer full exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing unsettled questions the writer should avoid taking up every gauntlet thrown down to him; refrain from polemical engagement until a full exposition can be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains his policy: 'I have made it a policy to avoid controversy as much as possible, even at the cost of being seriously misunderstood.' This is offered as a prudent methodological and rhetorical stance for scholarly work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ontogenetic/developmental evidence as analogue for phylogenetic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of individual development (infant and child emotional development, associations formed in nursery) can be used to support hypotheses about the historical/genetic formation of sentiments and beliefs in the race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author marshals infant reactions (smile at mother's laugh; cry at angry tones), nursery experiences, and the progressive aggregation of associations as empirical grounding for claims about how moral sentiments and space-intuitions develop historically. Use such developmental analogies cautiously but as substantive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish emotional genesis from intellectual generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral sentiments arise from complex aggregated associations of feelings (many varied experiences), not from consciously reasoned generalizations about utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists on a psychological distinction: 'the genesis of emotions is distinguished from the genesis of ideas.' Emotions are composed of 'enormously complex aggregates' producing 'a multitudinous, confused consciousness' — so explanations of moral feelings should appeal to associative and partly inherited emotional structures rather than to explicit rational calculation of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative (non-conscious) formation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of likes, dislikes, and moral repugnances can occur via habitual association of sensations and feelings without conscious belief in causal connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childhood jam taken after medicine becomes nauseous by association; cawing of rooks pleasant because associated with past gratifications. This supports hypotheses that sentimental dispositions can be formed and inherited as associations rather than as reflective beliefs.
